Breton Civil War, 1341-1343

The Breton Civil War, 1341-1343, was a dynastic dispute between two claimants to the Duchy of Brittany. It broke out after the death of Duke John III in 1341. The conflict was further complicated by the involvement of the French and English monarchs, leading to a larger conflict during the Hundred Years' War. The war ended in 1343 with the victory of Jean de Montfort, leading to a period of relative stability in the region.

The Breton Civil War was primarily caused by a dispute over the succession to the Duchy of Brittany. Duke John III died in 1341 without a male heir, leaving his wife Joanna of Montfort as the regent for their young son John. This led to a power struggle between two claimants: John of Montfort and Charles de Blois. The conflict was further fueled by the intervention of the French and English monarchs, each supporting a different claimant. John of Montfort was backed by Edward III of England, while Charles de Blois was supported by John II of France.

The key figures in the Breton Civil War include:
- John of Montfort: The English-backed claimant to the Duchy of Brittany.
- Charles de Blois: The French-backed claimant to the Duchy of Brittany.
- Jean de Montfort: The son of John of Montfort, who took command after his father's capture.
- Joanna of Montfort: The regent for her son John, who took command of the field army.
- Edward III of England: The English monarch who supported John of Montfort.
- John II of France: The French monarch who supported Charles de Blois.

The Breton Civil War ended in 1343 with the victory of Jean de Montfort and his English allies over Charles de Blois. This led to a period of relative stability in the Duchy of Brittany, with Jean de Montfort becoming the Duke.

The Breton Civil War was significant as it highlighted the complex political and military dynamics of the Hundred Years' War. It also demonstrated the influence of external powers, such as England and France, on the internal affairs of Brittany. The conflict further strained the relationship between the two countries and contributed to the ongoing tensions during the Hundred Years' War.

[![Image 2: Illustration depicting a medieval battle scene with knights in armor fighting near a castle, while a horse-drawn cart with a coffin-like structure passes nearby](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png/500px-Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png)

Funeral of [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), depicted in the Chronicles of [Jean Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart")

The **War of the Breton Succession** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _guerre de Succession de Bretagne_; [Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_language "Breton language"): _Brezel hêrezh dugelezh Breizh_) or **Breton Civil War** was a conflict between the [Counts of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_of_Blois "Counts of Blois") and the [Montforts of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfort_of_Brittany "Montfort of Brittany") for control of the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"), then a [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") of the [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France"). It was fought between 1341 and 12 April 1365.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_note-FritzeRobison2002-1) It is also known as the **War of the Two Joans** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _guerre des deux Jeannes_) due to the involvement of two rival duchesses of that name, [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") and [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_note-2)

The war formed an integral part of the early [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") due to the proxy involvement of the French and English monarchs in the conflict; the French supported the Blois (female heir) whilst the English backed the Montforts (male heir). The rival kings supported the duke of the principle opposite to their own claims to the French throne—the [Plantagenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Plantagenet "House of Plantagenet") having claimed it by female succession, and the [Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Valois "House of Valois") by male succession. Montfort was ultimately successful following the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") in 1364 but, in a surprising turn of events, pledged his loyalty to the king of France and not to the Plantagenet king of England who had supported him.

The Breton dukes had both a historical and ancestral connection to Britain and were also [earls of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earls_of_Richmond "Earls of Richmond") in [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire"). Duke [Arthur II of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany") married twice, first to Mary of Limoges (1275–1291), then to [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_of_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande of Dreux, Queen of Scotland") (1263–1322), countess of Montfort and widow of King [Alexander III of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_III_of_Scotland "Alexander III of Scotland"). From his first marriage, he had three sons, including his heir [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") and Guy, [count of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_and_dukes_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Counts and dukes of Penthièvre") (d. 1331). From Yolande, Arthur had another son, also named John, who became Count of Montfort. (See [Dukes of Brittany family tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Brittany_family_tree "Dukes of Brittany family tree").)

John III strongly disliked the children of his father's second marriage. He spent the first years of his reign attempting to have this marriage annulled and his half-siblings bastardized. When this failed, he tried to ensure that [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort") would never inherit the duchy. Since John III was childless, his heir of choice became [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), _la Boiteuse_, daughter of his younger brother Guy. In 1337 she married [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), the second son of a powerful French noble house whose mother's brother was King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). But in 1340, John III reconciled himself with his half-brother, and made a will that appointed John of Montfort the heir of Brittany. On 30 April 1341, John III died. His last words on the succession, uttered on his deathbed, were, "For God's sake leave me alone and do not trouble my spirit with such things".

First stage of the war
----------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=War_of_the_Breton_Succession&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: First stage of the war")]

Most of the nobility supported Charles of Blois, so if John of Montfort was to have any chance, it was dependent upon swift action before organized resistance could be made. John quickly took possession of the [ducal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke "Duke") capital [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") and then seized the Ducal treasury at [Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoges "Limoges"). By the middle of August, John of Montfort was in possession of most of the Duchy, the three principal cities of Nantes, [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") and [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes").

Up to this point, the succession crisis had been a purely internal affair. But to complicate things further, the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France had broken out four years earlier, in 1337. In 1341, there was a truce between the two countries, but there was little doubt that hostilities would be renewed when the truce ended in June 1342. Thus, when rumours reached [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") that John of Montfort had received English agents, the French Crown naturally took a more direct interest in their small neighbors situation. Charles of Blois became the official French candidate. Whatever had been his original intentions, John of Montfort was now forced to support [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") as King of France.

Edward III was bound by the truce not to take any offensive action in France. Nothing in it, however, hindered France from subduing rebellious vassals. In November, after a short siege and defeat at the [Battle of Champtoceaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux "Battle of Champtoceaux"), John of Montfort was forced to surrender at [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") by the citizens. He was offered safe conduct to negotiate a settlement with Charles of Blois, but when this led nowhere he was thrown in prison.

It now fell upon John's wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), to lead the Montfortist cause. Deeming her possessions in the east indefensible, she set up headquarters at [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont") in western Brittany but was driven into Brest and besieged, the siege being broken by the arrival of an English army under the [Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") at the [naval battle of Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Brest_(1342) "Battle of Brest (1342)") on 18 August 1342. Northampton then made his way inland and besieged Morlaix after an unsuccessful initial attack. The siege was lifted after the [battle of Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix") on 30 September. In Paris it was feared that Edward III would land at [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais") once the truce ran out. The major part of the French army was therefore withdrawn, and Charles of Blois was left to pursue his claim on his own. Charles soon proved himself to be an able soldier: Rennes and Vannes were taken and many of the Montfortist captains defected.

In late November, [Edward III arrived with his army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign,_1342%E2%80%931343 "Edward III's Breton campaign, 1342–1343") at [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"). He almost at once marched against Vannes. [The siege dragged on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieges_of_Vannes_(1342) "Sieges of Vannes (1342)") and a French army was assembled to meet him, but on 19 January 1343, before any major engagements could be fought, the two kings agreed the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"). Vannes was taken into papal custody. With John of Montfort in prison, his son an infant, and his wife recently gone mad, the places under Montfortist control were in practice administered from London, with a large permanent English garrison at Brest.

The truce was to last until 29 September 1346 with the hopes that in the meantime the disputes between the two kingdoms could be permanently settled, but in Brittany it made little difference. The truce bound the two kings and their followers, but Charles of Blois claimed to be fighting his own separate war and was therefore not bound by any truce. The brutal small-scale fighting continued at the same pace.

In Paris, John of Montfort was released from prison on 1 September 1343 in return for a huge bond and a promise to stay on his estates in the east. The English coastal garrisons held firm, but the Montfortist party continued to crumble. They had some successes, such as the expulsion of the papal custodians from Vannes, but with no unifying leadership, mostly they were reduced to pleading for men and money from London.

To hamper communication between Brest and Vannes, Charles of Blois laid siege to [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper,_Finist%C3%A8re "Quimper, Finistère") in early March 1344. The city fell by assault on 1 May and, as usual at that time, this meant the slaughter of civilians in huge numbers, estimated between 1,400 and 2,000. The English prisoners were held for ransom, but the Breton and Norman captives were dispatched to Paris where they were executed for treason. During the summer and autumn, the Montfortist party fell apart. Even those who had been John of Montfort's staunchest allies now considered it futile to continue the struggle. It, therefore, mattered little that in March 1345 John finally managed to escape to England. With no adherents of note of his own, he was now little more than a figurehead for English ambitions in Brittany.

Edward III decided to repudiate the truce in summer 1345, a year before it was due to run out. As part of his larger strategy, a force was dispatched to Brittany under the joint leadership of the [Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") and John of Montfort. Within a week of their landing in June, the English had their first victory when Sir [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth"), one of Northampton's lieutenants, raided central Brittany and defeated Charles of Blois at Cadoret near [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin").

The follow-up was less impressive. Further operations were delayed until July when Montfort attempted the recapture of Quimper. However, news had reached the French government that Edward's main campaign had been canceled and they were able to send reinforcements from Normandy. With his strengthened army, Charles of Blois broke the siege. Routed, Montfort fled back to Hennebont where he fell ill and died on 16 September. The heir to the Montfortist cause was his five-year-old son, [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany").

During the winter, Northampton fought a long and hard campaign with the apparent objective of seizing a harbour on the north side of the peninsula. Edward III had probably planned to land here with his main force during summer 1346. However, the English achieved very little for their efforts. Northern Brittany was Joan of Penthièvre's home region and resistance there was stiff.

In the end, Edward decided upon Normandy as the landing spot for his 1346 campaign. Northampton was recalled and Thomas Dagworth was appointed as deputy lieutenant. It was during a tour through the English strongholds on 9 June that Dagworth and his escort were trapped by Charles of Blois and his army near [Saint-Pol-de-Léon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Pol-de-L%C3%A9on "Saint-Pol-de-Léon"). They dug in on a hilltop and fought off all attacks until nightfall when Charles was forced to retreat leaving many of his wounded behind.

Tide turns against Charles
--------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=War_of_the_Breton_Succession&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Tide turns against Charles")]

[![Image 3: Medieval battle scene with knights on horseback and archers](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg/250px-Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg)

Capture of Charles of Blois

At this point events outside Brittany started to have an effect on the war. The French suffered a major defeat at the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") in 1346, and at Calais in 1347. Without French support, Charles of Blois gradually began to lose ground to the English captains. The memory of the massacre at Quimper increased his unpopularity, and Breton traders had an economic interest in strengthening links with England due to Brittany's strategic position between the Atlantic and English Channel. At the [Battle of La Roche-Derrien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_La_Roche-Derrien "Battle of La Roche-Derrien") in 1347, Charles was taken prisoner as he tried to recapture the town, which had just been taken by the English. He was jailed for five years in the Tower of London. The English now controlled Brest, Quimper, and Vannes.

Under pressure from [Pope Innocent VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Innocent_VI "Pope Innocent VI"), the English, French, and Bretons negotiated a peace, while both factions maintained an uneasy balance of power within the duchy. It was during this period that the [Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty") took place, a famous episode in medieval chivalry. Conflicts between the French and English strongholds of [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin") and [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel") were resolved in a duel between thirty Montfortist knights led by [Robert Bemborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bemborough "Robert Bemborough"), and thirty supporters of Charles de Blois led by [Jean de Beaumanoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_de_Beaumanoir "Jean de Beaumanoir"). The combat took place midway between the two towns on 26 March 1351. By nightfall the Anglo-Breton Montfortists had lost nine dead against six of the pro-French knights; the surviving Montfortists were forced to surrender. Though renowned at the time, and later highly romanticised, the combat had no effect on the outcome of the war.

[![Image 4: Painted image showing a medieval battlefield, in shades of white, blue, brown, and yellow, with dozens of soldiers on foot and horseback, some of whom are fighting](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg/250px-Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Le_Combat_des_Trente_(1857).jpg)

A 19th-century painting depicting the _[The Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Combat\_of\_the\_Thirty "The Combat of the Thirty")_ ([Octave Penguilly L'Haridon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_Penguilly_L%27Haridon "Octave Penguilly L'Haridon"), 1857)

Edward III signed the Treaty of Westminster on 1 March 1353, accepting Charles of Blois as Duke of Brittany if the latter undertook to pay a ransom of 300,000 crowns, and that Brittany signed a treaty of alliance "in perpetuity" with England; this alliance was to be sealed by the marriage of the Montfortist claimant John of Montfort (son of the earlier John of Montfort) with Edward's daughter Mary. The marriage required the approval of the King of France and a papal dispensation. [Charles de la Cerda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_la_Cerda "Charles de la Cerda"), the [Constable of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constable_of_France "Constable of France"), negotiated the deal, but [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre"), who needed to continue the war between England and France to maintain his own power, decided to intervene by assassinating the Constable. He then switched his support to France in exchange for territory. The treaty was negated, but Charles of Blois had been freed, and returned to Brittany as Duke.

[![Image 5: Medieval battle scene depicted with horses and soldiers engaged in combat, flags waving, and a sense of chaotic energy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg/250px-Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg)

The Battle of Auray, 1364

The situation remained in stalemate for some time, with Charles of Blois as _de facto_ Duke, but with significant territory still controlled by the Montfortists. Outside events again began to have an effect on the conflict. A plague struck France and the King himself was captured by the English at the [Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers") in 1356. The French state was virtually paralysed. In 1362, when the younger John de Montfort reached 22 years of age, King Edward permitted him to return to Brittany. His return was conditioned by a covenant not to marry without permission, given in pledge of several fortresses. On arrival, John attempted to reach agreement with Charles of Blois to make peace and share Brittany, but Charles's wife Joan urged him to resist and crush John.

The war resumed in 1363 when Charles de Blois, assisted by [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin"), had some successes, but when Bertrand left to take control of strongholds in Navarre and Normandy, Charles's advance halted at the unsuccessful siege of Bécherel. Another opportunity to negotiate an agreement arose, but again Joan blocked negotiations. John de Montfort moved to besiege [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray") with renowned English warlord [John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chandos "John Chandos"). Charles of Blois and Bertrand du Guesclin came to the rescue of the besieged city, but they were decisively defeated at the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") on 29 September 1364. This battle marked the end of this long conflict: Charles of Blois was killed and Joan of Penthièvre, finding herself a widow, saw her cause collapse. Du Guesclin was captured and [ransomed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom "Ransom") by Charles V for 100,000 [francs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franc "Franc").

Peace was concluded on 12 April 1365 by the [First Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_(1365) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)") which established John of Montfort as Duke of Brittany. He did not reject completely the claims of the Penthièvre family, and established the following law of succession in Brittany:

*   The Duchy would be transmitted from male to male in the family of Montfort.
*   In the absence of male offspring, it would switch to males of the family of Penthièvre.
*   Joan retained the prerogative of Penthièvre and the Viscouncy of Limoges.
*   She would also receive 10,000 livres of annual rent taken from the French territories of the enemy.

King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") did not oppose the elevation of John, fearing that he might declare homage to Edward of England, his protector and former father-in-law (Mary having died in 1361). In addition, France was clearly depleted in the context of the Hundred Years' War. He therefore recognized John as Duke. By this action, he won the friendship of the Breton nobility. In December 1366, he received the oath of the new duke who surprisingly did not pledge allegiance to Edward, recognizing Charles as his sovereign instead.

The provisions of the treaty were later repudiated by the Montfortists when a later duke, [John V, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_V,_Duke_of_Brittany "John V, Duke of Brittany") was kidnapped by the Penthièvres in 1420, in violation of the treaty. The Montfortists declared that the treaty had been broken, and as such were no longer required to accept its succession provisions. This became significant when [Francis II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Francis II, Duke of Brittany") failed to produce a male heir, allowing the duchy to pass to his daughter [Anne of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_of_Brittany "Anne of Brittany") in 1488.

*   **30 April 1341**: John III dies without heirs. Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois became Duchess and Duke of Brittany. John of Montfort refuses to accept and calls for the help of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England").
*   **1343**: John of Montfort is taken prisoner, but is released shortly afterwards. Charles tries to take advantage and attacks Hennebont, but the city is defended with success by [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), wife of Montfort. An English army relieves the siege and forces the Blois to a truce, broken shortly afterwards.
*   **1344**: Charles takes Quimper with the help of a French army, courtesy of King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), and slaughters 2000 civilians.
*   **1345**: John of Montfort fails to recover Quimper and dies. His ambitions over Brittany are inherited by his son [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"). His mother, Joan of Flanders, becomes the political and military commander of the Montfort faction.
*   **Between 1346 and 1364**, several minor battles are won and lost by both parts, several truces are signed and broken. Joan of Flanders becomes mentally ill and is institutionalized in a convent. 
    *   **27 March 1351**: [Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty")

*   **29 September 1364**: [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray"). [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin") and Charles of Blois are heavily defeated by John IV and the English warlord [John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chandos "John Chandos"). Charles is killed in action, ending the Blois pretensions in Brittany.
*   **1365**: John IV is recognized as Duke of Brittany and Joan of Penthièvre gives up any claim to the duchy in the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_(1365) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"). Surprisingly, the new duke declares himself as a vassal, not to the English king who helped him, but to King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France").

The [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession") was a dynastic dispute between two claimants to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") which broke out in May 1341, after the death of Duke [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"). A complicating factor was the ongoing [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"). [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") supported the claim to the duchy of his nephew, [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"); [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") backed the rival claimant, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"). John seized most of the fortified places in Brittany in 1341, but a French army sent to support Charles overran eastern Brittany and captured John in November. John's wife, [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), took command of her husband's field army, set up her two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy, and appealed for English military intervention. A [truce between France and England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was in place, but it was due to expire in June 1342.

In late May 1342 Charles led an army against the small but strongly walled port of [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont") where Joanna was based. Repeated assaults were rebuffed, but the delayed arrival of English reinforcements– caused by lack of shipping and bad weather– forced the Montfortists to retreat to the extreme west of Brittany. The English arrived in August, [relieved Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Brest_(1342) "Siege of Brest (1342)")– where Charles was again besieging Joanna– and inflicted a heavy defeat on Charles at the [battle of Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix"), the first land battle of the Hundred Years' War. Edward III arrived with further English reinforcements, besieged [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes"), and in turn overran most of Brittany. Attempts to reinforce or supply Edward from England failed and a French army greatly outnumbering the Anglo-Montfortist force was raised and advanced to [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit"), 18 miles (29 km) from the English camp. Philip entered into negotiations with Edward and the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"), which was supposed to pause hostilities for three-and-a-half years, was agreed on 19 January 1343.

A peace conference was arranged in [Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon "Avignon") where, mediated by [Pope Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI"), a treaty to permanently end the war was to be drafted. The conference did not convene until late 1344, due to English quibbling over the arrangements. The proposals made by each side were unacceptable to the other. Neither displayed any willingness to compromise, and the conference rapidly collapsed. After mutual provocations Edward formally renounced the truce on 15 June 1345 and full-scale war resumed. Despite the truce, the Breton Civil War had been grinding on as a disjointed and inconclusive series of petty sieges and skirmishes. The English and their Montfortist allies held almost the whole of Brittany by 1345. The Breton Civil War continued until 1365, the Hundred Years' War until 1453.

[![Image 2: a map of France showing only a small part of the south-west under English control](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg/250px-Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg)

France in 1328: English-controlled Gascony is shown in blue in the south west

Since the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest") of 1066, English monarchs had held titles and lands within France, the possession of which made them [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the kings of France. By the first quarter of the fourteenth century, the only sizeable French possession still held by the English in France was [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony") in the south west.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199039%E2%80%9340-1) Following a series of disagreements between [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") and [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), on 24 May 1337 Philip's [Great Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_du_Roi "Conseil du Roi") agreed that the lands held by Edward III in France should be taken back into Philip's hands on the grounds that Edward was in breach of his obligations as a vassal. This marked the start of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), which was to last 116 years.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990184-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger200479-3)

On 26 January 1340 Edward formally [claimed the French throne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne"). The immediate effect was to allow the [Flemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people") to join his cause without technically disowning their fealty to the French crown and therefore becoming rebels. The extent to which Edward considered the claim more than a negotiating position is unclear. In June the French navy was annihilated by the English fleet at the [battle of Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sluys "Battle of Sluys") and in July Edward [invaded north-east France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tournaisis_campaign_of_1340 "Tournaisis campaign of 1340") at the head of a large, heavily subsidised, allied army. The allies [laid siege to Tournai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Tournai_(1340) "Siege of Tournai (1340)") on 1 August. On 7 September the French army arrived, but Philip held it back to ensure there was no risk of a battle occurring. He was probably aware that the allied army was falling apart, with the English unable to pay their allies what they had been promised, or even to feed them. Negotiations for a pause in the fighting were opened, mediated by emissaries of [Pope Benedict XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XII "Pope Benedict XII"). The [Truce of Espléchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was rapidly agreed, to last from 25 September 1340 to 24 June 1341. The allied armies left France thereafter.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200235%E2%80%9336-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006299%E2%80%93300-5) The English Crown, bankrupt, was unable to meet its commitments, and Edward fled the continent to avoid his creditors.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1998233-6)

Civil war in Brittany
---------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Civil war in Brittany")]

[Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany") was a province of France, but although the [dukes of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Brittany "Dukes of Brittany") were vassals of the [French kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_kings "French kings") they governed the duchy as independent rulers.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199017,_34%E2%80%9335-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200662-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones19888%E2%80%9311-9) Nevertheless, when the Hundred Years' War broke out in 1337 between France and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") the duke of Brittany, [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") (r. 1312–1341), fought alongside his [feudal lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_lord "Feudal lord") the king of France. John III died on 30 April 1341, leaving a disputed succession, with both his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), and his younger half-brother, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), claiming the duchy. Joan's claim was exercised through her husband, [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), a well-connected and militarily oriented French nobleman who was also a nephew of King Philip of France.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990370%E2%80%93371-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199966%E2%80%9367-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202047%E2%80%9349-12)

On John III's death John of Montfort acted quickly and installed friendly garrisons in most of the towns and castles of Brittany by August.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-13) The [Parlement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlement_of_Paris "Parlement of Paris") was the supreme judicial authority in France[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-13) and on 7 September, at Philip's urging, it declared that Charles of Blois was the legitimate successor to John III.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007203-14) Philip found the idea of having a relative as the duke attractive because it would bring the traditionally semi-autonomous province more firmly under royal control. He was willing to commit considerable military resources to achieve this and despatched an army, commanded by his eldest son, [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France"), to support Charles.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-15)

This army overran all of eastern Brittany except [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") and took John of Montfort prisoner.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389-16)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-19) John's wife, [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), was in Rennes when news of John's capture arrived. She acted decisively, recalled the field army from western Brittany, took command[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21) and moved to [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), a small but strongly walled town with access to the sea. From there Joanna retained control of most of western Brittany[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390-20) and set up her two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433%E2%80%9334-22) She despatched her senior counsellor, [Amaury of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaury_of_Clisson "Amaury of Clisson"), to [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III "Edward III"), the English king, with the ducal treasury to encourage English military intervention and waited on events.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21)

On 21 February 1342 Edward sealed a treaty to support the Montfort cause as an extension of the war with France.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990390-24) Edward saw the opportunity to set up a ruler in Brittany at least partly under his control; this could provide access to Breton ports which would greatly aid England's naval war and give ready entry to France for English armies.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-15)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011109-25) In May 1342 [Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clement_VI "Clement VI") became pope. He was strongly pro-French and had previously been one of Philip's senior advisers. He despatched two cardinals to attempt to broker a permanent settlement of the Anglo-French war. The following month they were well received by Philip in Paris; Edward, on the other hand, would not even allow them to cross [the Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Channel "The Channel").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990395%E2%80%93396-26)

English intervention
--------------------

English reinforcements took a long time to arrive and in May 1342 Rennes fell, allowing Charles to march on Hennebont, part of a general offensive to push his area of control westward.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990391,_393-29)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011109%E2%80%93111-30) On arrival at Hennebont several units of Charles's army advanced against orders and attacked some of the town's defenders who were formed up outside its gate. More troops were pulled into this fight before the French were pushed back in a disorderly retreat. The Montfortists pursued, inflicting many casualties and burning the French camp. According to a contemporary account Joanna rode through the suburbs in full armour encouraging the fighting men.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21) Two days later the French launched a series of better-planned assaults on the town's walls, but all were repulsed with losses.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201436-31) The main French force moved on, leaving a detachment to carry out a regular siege in an attempt to starve the town into surrender.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990394%E2%80%93395-32)

A fleet of French and mercenary [galleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley "Galley") cruised off the north Breton coast, but there was so little English naval activity that they were beached and their crews went ashore to fight as infantry. Edward planned to land in Brittany himself in June with a substantial force, but extreme difficulty in assembling ships,[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-35) despite draconian measures taken by Admiral [Robert Morley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Morley,_2nd_Baron_Morley "Robert Morley, 2nd Baron Morley"), and then contrary winds, caused this date to be repeatedly put back.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990391,_393-29)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011109%E2%80%93111-30)

While waiting for English reinforcements the flow of events went against the Montfortists in the face of Charles's huge military superiority. Having taken Vannes,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-36) he moved on to besiege Auray and, again, Hennebont; both fell. By August little was left to Jeanne's forces, most of whom were besieged in the western port of [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France") by a large army and blockaded from the sea by 14 mercenary [Genoese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa") galleys.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990393,_397%E2%80%93398-37) Brest was on the brink of surrender when the English arrived on 18 August. Their fleet of 140 converted merchantmen and an unknown number of galleys took the Genoese galleys by surprise and 11 were burnt.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004100-38)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-36)

The English ships carried 1,350 men,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004100-38) a force far inferior to that of the French besieging Brest. But, seeing so many English ships crowded into the [Brest Roads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roadstead_of_Brest "Roadstead of Brest") and the English [vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanguard "Vanguard") disembarking onto the beach, they anticipated an attack by a vast host. Charles promptly broke off the siege and withdrew 65 kilometres (40 mi), abandoning western Brittany, where the populace strongly favoured the Montfort cause.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-39)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990399%E2%80%93400-40) Part of Charles' force withdrew along the south coast of Brittany, but the bulk of the army accompanied him to [Guingamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guingamp "Guingamp").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-41) Here he concentrated his forces and called up local levies.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-39) The English were commanded by [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton"), who was reinforced by 800 men under [Robert of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois") a few days after landing. He also absorbed several other small English forces and an unknown number of John of Montfort's Breton partisans.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-41) Northampton's first mission was to secure a port for the main English army to disembark at.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-41)

[![Image 19: A pen and ink drawing of the head and shoulders of a bearded man in early modern style](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/CarlosIdebritania.jpg/240px-CarlosIdebritania.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CarlosIdebritania.jpg)

Charles of Blois as envisaged in 1621[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBritannica2018-42)

The English marched 30 miles (50 km) from Brest to Morlaix, a port on the north coast of Brittany with strong fortifications and a secure harbour, and laid siege to it.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-39)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990399%E2%80%93401-43) Edward's contingent was still in England waiting for the ships which had transported Northampton's echelon to return. The French mistakenly believed this army would be used in north-east France, probably disembarking in [Picardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picardy "Picardy"). A French army was gathered to confront this imagined threat, including many men transferred from Brittany. Charles became aware his force greatly outnumbered the English, despite the detachments to Picardy, and took his army west in an attempt to relieve Morlaix. [[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401%E2%80%93402-44)

Warned of this, the English carried out a night march and prepared a defensive position on the Guingamp-Morlaix road.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199971%E2%80%9372-45) When they sighted the English position, the French deployed into three divisions, one behind the other.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-46)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199972%E2%80%9373-47) The first of these, probably made up of Breton [levies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_levies "Feudal levies"), advanced and was shot to pieces by the English archers using [longbows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbow "Longbow"); it then broke without making contact.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-48)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-49) The second division, of French and Breton [men-at-arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men-at-arms "Men-at-arms"), attacked but their charge was halted when they fell into a camouflaged ditch in front of the English position. Presented with a large, close-range target the English archers inflicted many casualties.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-49)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-50) About 200 French cavalry made their way over the ditch and came to grips with the English men-at-arms, who were fighting on foot. This band was cut off by the English and all were killed or captured.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-48)

Northampton was concerned that the English archers were running out of arrows and that the ditch was so full of dead and wounded men and horses as to be ineffective as an obstacle. Therefore, when the third French division was seen to be preparing to attack the English withdrew into a wood to their rear.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222%E2%80%93223-51) The French were unable to force their way in, so they surrounded it and besieged the English, possibly for several days. Northampton broke out with a night attack and returned to Morlaix.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19996-52)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975-53) Charles gave up his attempt to relieve the town and retreated.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975-53) This was the first major land battle of the Hundred Years' War[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-54)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-49)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990483-55) and the tactics used foreshadowed those of both the French and the English for the rest of the 1340s.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19996-52)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975%E2%80%9376,_112%E2%80%93113-56)

On 6 October Edward abandoned his [siege train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_(military) "Train (military)") on the beach and set sail from England with those troops he was able to embark onto the available shipping. They reached Brittany after a storm-wracked three-week passage.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011112%E2%80%93113-57)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401,_403-58) After concentrating at Brest, the English and Montfortist force moved on the major city of [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes"), the second most populous settlement in Brittany, with a good harbour and walls. From Vannes a strong detachment could control much of southern Brittany. On 7 November both the navy and the army set off. The fleet was depleted by the desertion of most of its ships; their masters and crews were unhappy at not being paid and at being forced out to sea in dangerous winter weather.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-59)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990403%E2%80%93404-60)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFr%C3%A9laut200535-61) Those left sailed to Vannes, enduring a winter storm en route. They attempted to take the town with a surprise attack; this came close to success but was defeated.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990404%E2%80%93405-62)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-59)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004102-63) In England the [King's Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curia_regis "Curia regis") attempted to organise a further fleet to carry supplies and reinforcements. Fifty-six ships sailed on or after 3 November carrying 600 men, but were driven ashore in the [Isles of Scilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isles_of_Scilly "Isles of Scilly") by further storms. They and 800 men who had not sailed waited for a break in the weather, fruitlessly: they were finally [stood down](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/stand_down "wikt:stand down") in February 1343.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406-64)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-59)

The main Anglo-Breton army marched unopposed 120 miles (190 km) through southern Brittany and on 29 November attempted to take Vannes by storm. The French garrison had been newly reinforced and repelled this assault; a regular siege began.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990405%E2%80%93406-65) The siege did not require the entire army and large detachments were sent on [chevauchees](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/chevauchee "wikt:chevauchee") across eastern Brittany to devastate the region and capture the fortified places. The outskirts of [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan") and the area around [Dol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dol-de-Bretagne "Dol-de-Bretagne") were devastated, 100 miles (160 km) north of Vannes.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990405%E2%80%93406-65)[Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel"), [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit") and [Redon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redon,_Ille-et-Vilaine "Redon, Ille-et-Vilaine") were captured and [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes"), the ducal capital, was besieged.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200660,_207-66) Increasing numbers of Breton knights and lords switched their allegiance to the Montfortist cause. However, there were fewer than 5,000 English troops in Brittany, and the term of service of many was running out.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406-64) No food supplies were arriving for Edward by sea, and although he sent out foraging columns over a broad area, living off the land in winter yielded thin returns. Edward's army was in difficulty.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007206-67)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004102-63)

[![Image 20: See caption](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG/250px-Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG)

The commemorative plaque on the ruins of the [Chapel of the Madeleine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_the_Madeleine,_Malestroit "Chapel of the Madeleine, Malestroit") where the truce was sealed,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-68) reads: "Historic ruins of the Magdalene chapel, where was signed on 19th January 1343 during the Hundred Years' war by representatives of the English and French realms, the Truce of Malestroit, in the presence of Papal legates the Cardinals of Clermont and Prenets."[[note 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-70)

The French were perturbed by Edward's landing in Brittany, when he was expected to invade further east, and by his taking the field so late in the season, when their armies had been disbanded. During November they struggled to put together an army and to accumulate sufficient supplies to feed and equip it. The army was based at the major French supply centre of [Angers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angers "Angers")[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990386,_406%E2%80%93407-71) with John, Duke of Normandy, again in command.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-68) There are no contemporary figures on the size of the French army, but it was several times larger than the Anglo-Breton force.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007207-72) It was 14 December before the French began the 50-mile (80 km) journey west to the Breton border. Edward was sufficiently alarmed to invite the two cardinals he had brushed off in the summer to present their credentials. They had been observing events from [Avranches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avranches "Avranches"), just over the Breton border, and were allowed no closer than Malestroit, 18 miles (29 km) from the main English camp. Edward suspected that details of everything they saw would be passed on to the French and took great care not to betray the small size and poor state of his army.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406%E2%80%93407-73)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-68)

Once started, the French advance was rapid; it was Christmas Day (25 December) 1342[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199984-74) when the French relieved Nantes. Redon, Ploërmel and Malestroit were recaptured during early January and the French encamped around the latter. The two cardinals were probably in Malestroit when it fell to the French, on or shortly after 10 January.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990386,_406%E2%80%93407-71) As in 1340 the French were content to threaten the English, without moving close enough for serious fighting to be a possibility. With both sides disinclined to commit to battle, negotiations were entered into.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-75) Philip VI set up his court at Redon from where he sent emissaries to the cardinals. By 19 January 1343 the terms of a truce had been agreed and it was sealed; the break in hostilities was to last until 29 September 1346.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990407%E2%80%93408-76)

The historian [Jonathan Sumption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Sumption,_Lord_Sumption "Jonathan Sumption, Lord Sumption") describes the terms as "astonishingly favourable" to the English.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990407%E2%80%93408-76) Both France and England were to retain the territory they held when the truce came into effect: this applied to Brittany, Gascony, [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") and [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409-77) Vannes was to be held by the papacy for the duration of the truce, Philip was to immediately free John of Montfort[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007207-72) and there was a general exchange of prisoners.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988208,_n._30-78)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-79) Both monarchs pledged to negotiate a treaty to permanently end the war, in [Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon "Avignon"), then the [seat of the Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy "Avignon Papacy"); with the process to be mediated by Clement. In reality each saw the truce as a mere pause and neither intended to negotiate in good faith; the truce had only been agreed because each king felt it was beneficial to him.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990408-80)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006110-81)

[![Image 21: a water colour image of the head and shoulders of a man wearing a white papal hat](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/01_Cl%C3%A9ment_VI_%28Fresque_de_la_chapelle_Saint-Martial_du_palais_des_papes%29.jpg/250px-01_Cl%C3%A9ment_VI_%28Fresque_de_la_chapelle_Saint-Martial_du_palais_des_papes%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:01_Cl%C3%A9ment_VI_(Fresque_de_la_chapelle_Saint-Martial_du_palais_des_papes).jpg)

Pope Clement VI, pictured on the wall of the Chapel of Saint-Martial in the [Papal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_des_Papes "Palais des Papes") in Avignon. Clement commissioned the decoration of the chapel, which was completed during his lifetime.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTELuyster2011334-82)

Edward left for England, enduring another winter storm which scattered the fleet, sinking several ships, He arrived on 1 March.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007209-83) Philip believed that with the fighting ended, all the English would leave for home, as they had left north-east France after the Truce of Espléchin. He was mistaken, and the Breton Civil War ground on in a series of petty skirmishes, despite the truce.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-75)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-84) The English and their Montfortist allies held almost the whole of Brittany by 1345.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoskins201113-85)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESadler2013211-86) John of Montfort was not released until September, despite the treaty's stipulations.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409,_432-87) Late in 1343 the citizens of Vannes rose against the Pope's authority, expelled his garrison and delivered the town to the English, who held it until the end of the Breton Civil War in 1364.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990432-88)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFr%C3%A9laut200535-61)

The English did not trust Clement and repeatedly delayed sending delegates to the envisaged peace talks. When the conference finally convened in late 1344 the proposals made by each side were unacceptable to the other, with neither displaying any willingness to compromise, and it rapidly collapsed.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200639-89) Neither monarch took the provisions of the truce agreement seriously; the fighting had continued much as before in Brittany and Gascony. Edward was planning another major invasion of France long before the truce was due to expire in September 1346.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-79) During the summer of 1343 [Olivier of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_IV_de_Clisson "Olivier IV de Clisson"), a senior Breton lord, was invited from England to a tournament on French soil. As he was protected by the treaty he attended, but on the orders of the French king was arrested for treason and executed without trial.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoveBiget2013131-90)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBordonove200674-91) Edward formally renounced the truce on 15 June 1345, at which Gascony [reverted to full-scale war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascon_campaign_of_1345 "Gascon campaign of 1345").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-79)

Edward personally led another expedition to France in 1346, this time [landing in Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%A9cy_campaign "Crécy campaign").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006xxxvi%E2%80%93xxxvii,_39-92) His army was wholly English and Welsh and it laid waste to a 40-mile-wide (64 km) strip of some of the richest lands in France to within 2 miles (3 km) of Paris, [sacking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looting "Looting") many towns on the way. On 26 August 1346 Philip was finally provoked into attacking at the [battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy"), where the French were defeated with a heavy loss of life.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200239%E2%80%9340-93)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006105%E2%80%93106-94)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2014252,_257-95) In the aftermath of this battle the English [laid siege to the port of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Calais_(1346%E2%80%931347) "Siege of Calais (1346–1347)"), which fell in August 1347. The [Truce of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Calais "Truce of Calais") was subsequently sealed on 28 September; originally due to expire on 7 July 1348, it was repeatedly extended until 1355, when full-scale war broke out once again.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200673%E2%80%9375-96)

Joanna of Montfort travelled to England in 1343 and took no further part in the war, dying in September 1374. She stayed in Tickhill Castle and it was given out at the time that she had gone insane; this is accepted by most historians although it has been suggested that she was confined for political reasons, rather than because of mental illness.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409-77)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarpy2019section_%22political_prisoner%22-97) John of Montfort died in 1345,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-36) but the Breton Civil War continued as a disjointed and inconclusive sequence of sieges, skirmishes and truces, frequently as part of the Hundred Years' War. The eastern and southern parts of Brittany were mostly held by the French, who continued to strongly support Charles of Blois, while western and northern Brittany continued to be largely Montfort or English controlled.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-54) Charles of Blois was killed in 1364 at the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") and his army decisively defeated. The next year his widow, Joan of Penthièvre, signed the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_(1365) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"), recognising John of Montfort's son as Duke of Brittany, which ended the war.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-75)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-84)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1999106-98)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200692%E2%80%9393-99) The Hundred Years' War continued until 1453, when it ended in a French victory.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006l-100)
